questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: Under ASC 250, a change in accounting principle is generally accounted for using which approach?

answers.text: Retrospective approach — all prior periods presented are restated to reflect the new principle, and the cumulative effect on periods not presented is recorded as an adjustment to the opening balance of retained earnings
Prospective approach — the new principle is applied only to current and future periods
Modified retrospective approach — the cumulative effect is recorded in current-period net income as a special item
No restatement is permitted — companies must continue with their original accounting principle once adopted

explanations.a: ASC 250-10-45-5 requires retrospective application when an entity changes an accounting principle. All prior periods presented in the financial statements are revised to reflect the new principle. The cumulative effect on all periods prior to those presented is reported as an adjustment to the opening balance of retained earnings (or net assets, or other applicable equity account) of the earliest period presented. This restated presentation allows users to compare periods on a consistent basis.
explanations.b: Prospective treatment is generally reserved for changes in accounting estimates — not changes in accounting principle. Principles require retrospective application to enhance comparability.
explanations.c: The modified retrospective approach (recording cumulative effect only in the current period) is specifically associated with certain standard transitions (e.g., ASC 606, ASC 842) rather than voluntary principle changes under ASC 250.
explanations.d: Companies can and do change accounting principles when required by a new standard or when they can justify the change as preferable. Once a principle is adopted, it is generally continued — but changes are permitted under specific circumstances.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company changes depreciation method from declining balance to straight-line for all existing assets. This is classified as

answers.text: A change in accounting estimate effected by a change in accounting principle — accounted for prospectively in current and future periods
A change in accounting principle requiring retrospective restatement of all prior periods
An error correction requiring a prior period adjustment to retained earnings
A change in reporting entity requiring restatement of all historical periods

explanations.a: ASC 250-10-45-17 classifies depreciation method changes (e.g., declining balance to straight-line) as changes in accounting estimate effected by a change in accounting principle. Because depreciation methods inherently involve estimating how an asset's economic benefits are consumed, a method change reflects revised assumptions about the pattern of consumption. These are accounted for prospectively — applied to the current period and future periods — without restating prior periods. The change is disclosed in the notes including the justification that the new method is preferable.
explanations.b: Depreciation method changes are specifically categorized as changes in estimate effected by a change in principle — not pure principle changes requiring full retrospective restatement.
explanations.c: An error correction addresses prior mistakes (mathematical errors, misapplication of GAAP, oversight of facts). A deliberate method change to a preferable method is not an error.
explanations.d: A change in reporting entity (e.g., presenting consolidated statements for the first time) is a different category with its own rules. A depreciation method change affects only the method of allocating cost — not the reporting entity.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company discovers in Year 3 that it failed to record $200,000 of accrued wages expense at the end of Year 1 (wages were paid in Year 2). The error is material. Year 1 and Year 2 comparative financial statements are being presented with Year 3. How is this error corrected?

answers.text: Restate Year 1 financial statements to include the $200,000 wages expense; adjust the beginning retained earnings balance for Year 2 (if Year 1 is not presented) or restate Year 1 directly; disclose the nature, effect, and reasons for the restatement
Record a $200,000 expense in Year 3 — errors are corrected in the period discovered
Disclose the error in Year 3 footnotes with no balance sheet or income statement adjustment
Adjust Year 2 opening retained earnings by $200,000 regardless of whether Year 1 is presented

explanations.a: ASC 250-10-45-23 requires correction of material errors in previously issued financial statements by restating the affected periods. Since Year 1 is presented comparatively, the Year 1 financial statements are restated: wages expense increases $200,000; wages payable increases $200,000 (or decreases retained earnings at year-end Year 1). Year 2 is also affected — the wages payable would have been paid in Year 2, so Year 2 is corrected to remove any related misstatement. Required disclosures include the nature of the error, the effect on income and equity for each period, and that prior periods have been restated.
explanations.b: Errors are not corrected prospectively (in the discovery period) under GAAP. Material errors require retrospective restatement of the periods in which they occurred.
explanations.c: Footnote disclosure alone is insufficient for a material error — the financial statements themselves must be restated.
explanations.d: If Year 1 is presented, the restatement directly corrects Year 1 — not merely Year 2's opening balance. Both approaches are possible depending on which years are presented, but since Year 1 is presented, it must be directly restated.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A change in the estimated useful life of a depreciable asset is accounted for

answers.text: Prospectively — the remaining book value (net of salvage) is depreciated over the revised remaining useful life; no restatement of prior periods
Retrospectively — all prior periods must be restated to reflect the revised estimate
As a prior period adjustment — the cumulative effect of the change is recorded in opening retained earnings
As an extraordinary item — changes in estimates that are unusual and infrequent require special classification

explanations.a: ASC 250-10-45-17 requires changes in accounting estimates to be recognized in the period of change and future periods if affected — never by restating prior periods. For a change in asset useful life: the remaining depreciable base (book value minus salvage value) at the date of change is divided by the revised remaining useful life. Future depreciation is recalculated using the new rate. This prospective approach reflects that the estimate was reasonable when originally made — it has simply been updated based on new information.
explanations.b: Changes in accounting estimates are never retrospectively restated — they are accounted for prospectively. Retrospective restatement is reserved for principle changes and error corrections.
explanations.c: Prior period adjustments (to opening retained earnings) are used only for error corrections and certain specific standard transitions — not for routine estimate changes.
explanations.d: Extraordinary item classification was eliminated by ASU 2015-01. Changes in estimates were never classified as extraordinary even before that amendment.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: When a company presents comparative financial statements and discovers an immaterial error in a prior period, what is the appropriate accounting treatment?

answers.text: The error may be corrected in the current period without restating prior periods — immaterial errors do not require restatement; the cumulative correction flows through current-period income
Full retrospective restatement is still required — all errors must be corrected regardless of materiality
The error must be disclosed in footnotes but cannot be corrected in either the current or prior periods
The immaterial error is ignored entirely — immaterial items have no accounting consequence whatsoever

explanations.a: For immaterial errors, an entity may correct the error in the current period by including the correction in current-period income. This avoids the cost and effort of full restatement when the amounts would not affect users' decisions. The correction appears in the income statement as an adjustment (often disclosed separately if it is significant enough to warrant explanation). This practical approach reflects GAAP's materiality threshold — financial statements do not need to be perfectly precise when corrections would not change the conclusions of reasonable users.
explanations.b: Materiality governs the accounting treatment for errors. Only material errors require full retrospective restatement. Immaterial errors have a simpler correction method.
explanations.c: Immaterial errors can be corrected — in the current period or, if impracticable, disclosed with the correction flowing through current income. Complete non-correction would misstate the current period.
explanations.d: While immaterial items have reduced accounting consequences, they are not wholly ignored. The error is still corrected — just in the current period rather than through restatement.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company switches from LIFO to FIFO inventory costing. Under the retrospective approach, the cumulative effect of the change increases retained earnings by $1,200,000 (after tax). The current year's income under FIFO is $300,000 higher than it would have been under LIFO. How are these amounts presented?

answers.text: $1,200,000 and $300,000 are both recognized in current-year net income as a combined $1,500,000 gain
The $1,200,000 cumulative effect is an extraordinary item; the $300,000 is in continuing operations
The $1,200,000 is reported in OCI; the $300,000 higher income appears in net income

The $1,200,000 cumulative effect adjusts the opening balance of retained earnings for the earliest period presented; the $300,000 higher income is reflected in the current-period income statement through normal operations under the new FIFO method — prior periods are also restated to FIFO basis

explanations.a: The cumulative effect is not recognized in current-year net income — under the retrospective approach, it adjusts the opening retained earnings of the earliest period presented and prior periods are restated.
explanations.b: Extraordinary item classification was eliminated by ASU 2015-01. The cumulative effect of accounting principle changes no longer appears as an extraordinary item.
explanations.c: Accounting principle changes do not flow through OCI. The cumulative effect adjusts retained earnings directly; the current-year income difference flows through the income statement in normal operations.
explanations.d: Under retrospective application: (1) All prior periods presented are restated from LIFO to FIFO basis — cost of goods sold, income taxes, and net income are revised for each prior period; (2) The cumulative effect on all periods prior to those presented ($1,200,000 net of tax) is an adjustment to the opening retained earnings of the earliest period presented — it does not go through current-year income; (3) The current year's income under FIFO ($300,000 higher) simply reflects normal FIFO results — no special presentation is needed beyond using FIFO throughout the income statement. This approach ensures all periods shown are on a consistent FIFO basis.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: An entity changes from the cash basis to the accrual basis of accounting. Accrual-basis net income would have been $180,000 higher than cash-basis net income for all prior years combined. This year, accrual-basis income is $25,000 higher than cash-basis. Assuming retrospective application is practicable, how is the $180,000 cumulative effect presented?

answers.text: Recognized in current-year net income — cumulative effects of principle changes are always in the current period
Allocated proportionally to each prior year presented based on relative revenues
Deferred and amortized over future periods as a deferred credit

As a prior period adjustment: the $180,000 (net of tax) increases opening retained earnings of the earliest period presented; each prior year presented is restated on the accrual basis; the $25,000 current-year difference is included in current-year income on the accrual basis

explanations.a: Cumulative effects of principle changes are not recognized in current-year net income under the retrospective approach — they adjust opening retained earnings.
explanations.b: Proportional allocation to prior years is not the correct mechanism. Each prior year is restated to its actual accrual-basis results, with any remaining pre-presentation cumulative effect going to opening retained earnings.
explanations.c: Deferred credit treatment was the prior GAAP approach (pre-SFAS 154) — current GAAP requires retrospective restatement, not deferral.
explanations.d: The retrospective approach requires: (1) Restate each prior year presented to accrual-basis income — adjusting revenues, expenses, receivables, and payables for each presented year; (2) The $180,000 cumulative pre-presentation effect (net of tax) is added to opening retained earnings of the earliest period presented — a direct equity adjustment bypassing the income statement; (3) Current-year income ($25,000 higher on accrual basis) is included in the income statement as part of normal operations. Full disclosures explain the nature of the change, the reason it is preferable, and the effect on each period.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A change in accounting principle is justified under ASC 250 only when

answers.text: It is required by a newly issued GAAP standard OR the entity can demonstrate the new principle is preferable — voluntary changes require a justification of preferability
It results in higher reported net income — companies may change principles when the change increases profitability
Management decides a different method would be simpler to implement — administrative convenience justifies principle changes
At least one year has elapsed since adoption of the original principle — the one-year waiting period satisfies the change requirement

explanations.a: ASC 250-10-45-2 permits a change in accounting principle only when: (1) mandated by a new GAAP pronouncement (e.g., a new FASB ASU requires adoption); or (2) the entity can demonstrate that the alternative principle is preferable for its particular circumstances. Preferability requires substantive justification — such as better matching the economics of the entity's business, industry-wide change to a different method, or more faithful representation of the entity's financial position. Administrative ease or income effects alone are insufficient.
explanations.b: Income maximization is not a permitted justification for changing accounting principles. Self-serving changes without substantive business rationale would undermine the reliability of financial reporting.
explanations.c: Administrative convenience is not a recognized basis for changing accounting principles. The change must improve the relevance or reliability of financial information.
explanations.d: No waiting period exists between adoption and permissible change — the issue is whether the change is justified, not how long ago the original adoption occurred.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: Under ASC 450, a loss contingency is accrued when

answers.text: The loss is both probable (likely to occur) and the amount can be reasonably estimated
The loss is possible — any chance of occurring triggers accrual
Legal counsel has formally advised that the company will lose — only attorney opinions trigger accrual
The loss is certain — only definite losses are accrued

explanations.a: ASC 450-20-25-2 establishes two conditions for accruing a loss contingency: (1) Probable — it is probable that a liability has been incurred based on information available before the financial statements are issued; and (2) Reasonably estimable — the amount of the loss can be reasonably estimated. Both conditions must be met. If only one condition is met (probable but not estimable, or estimable but only possible), no accrual is made — disclosure may be required instead.
explanations.b: 'Possible' (reasonably possible) contingencies require disclosure only — not accrual. Accrual requires the higher threshold of 'probable.'
explanations.c: Attorney advice is relevant evidence for assessing probability, but it is not the sole trigger. Management exercises judgment using all available information — including legal counsel opinions, industry experience, and specific facts.
explanations.d: Certainty is not required — the threshold is 'probable,' which means likely to occur but not guaranteed. Waiting for certainty would delay recognition beyond the appropriate period.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company is being sued for $5,000,000. Legal counsel believes there is a 25% chance of losing the suit. What is the appropriate accounting treatment?

answers.text: Accrue a loss of $5,000,000 — any litigation requires full accrual
Accrue a loss of $1,250,000 — probability-weighted expected loss (25% × $5,000,000)
No accrual and no disclosure — only probable losses are reported
Accrue nothing; disclose the contingency in the notes — a 25% probability is 'reasonably possible' (not probable), requiring disclosure but not accrual

explanations.a: A 25% probability does not meet the 'probable' threshold under ASC 450. Accrual is not appropriate.
explanations.b: Probability-weighted expected value is not the measurement approach under ASC 450 for accrual decisions. The threshold is qualitative ('probable'), not a mathematical weighting. If accrual were appropriate (probable and estimable), the amount accrued would be management's best estimate — not a probability-weighted amount.
explanations.c: 'Remote' contingencies require no accrual or disclosure. 'Reasonably possible' (25%) requires disclosure even without accrual. Omitting disclosure would violate ASC 450.
explanations.d: A 25% probability is 'reasonably possible' (more than remote but less than probable). Under ASC 450-20-50-3, reasonably possible contingencies require disclosure of the nature of the contingency and the range of possible loss (or a statement that an estimate cannot be made) — but no accrual. The disclosure allows users to assess the risk without overstating the liability.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company wins a lawsuit and expects to receive $800,000. The award has been issued by the court but the defendant has appealed. How should the gain contingency be reported?

answers.text: Disclose the contingent gain in the notes without recognition — gain contingencies are not recognized until the cash is actually received or the gain is realized
Recognize $800,000 as revenue immediately — the court has ruled in the company's favor
Recognize $800,000 in OCI as an unrealized gain — similar to AFS security gains
Recognize $800,000 as a deferred gain amortized over three years

explanations.a: ASC 450-30-25-1 prohibits recognizing gain contingencies before they are actually realized. Unlike loss contingencies (which are accrued when probable and estimable to reflect conservatism), gain contingencies follow a higher bar: recognition only when received or when realization is assured beyond reasonable doubt. The pending appeal creates uncertainty about ultimate collection, reinforcing the need to disclose rather than recognize. The notes describe the nature of the contingency and the potential amount without recording the gain.
explanations.b: Despite the favorable court ruling, the appeal creates uncertainty. Even without an appeal, gain contingencies are recognized only when realized — not merely when probable.
explanations.c: Gain contingencies are not OCI items — they are disclosed in notes until realized, at which point they are recognized in net income.
explanations.d: Deferred gain treatment does not apply here. Once realized (appeal resolved, payment received), the full gain is recognized — there is no amortization.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company guarantees a subsidiary's $3,000,000 bank loan. Under ASC 460, how should this guarantee be initially recognized by the guarantor?

answers.text: No entry — contingent liabilities are only disclosed in footnotes until payment becomes probable
Debit Guarantee Expense $3,000,000; Credit Guarantee Liability $3,000,000 — the full guaranteed amount is immediately expensed
Record a contingent loss only if the subsidiary's default is probable — same criteria as other loss contingencies

Record the fair value of the guarantee obligation as a liability (and corresponding asset or expense at inception) — ASC 460 requires initial recognition at fair value for guarantees issued after January 1, 2003

explanations.a: ASC 460 requires initial recognition of guarantee obligations — they are not merely footnote items.
explanations.b: Recognizing the full guaranteed amount as an immediate expense overstates the liability. The guarantee creates an obligation to stand ready, not to pay $3,000,000 immediately.
explanations.c: For new guarantees, the fair value recognition requirement applies immediately at inception — regardless of whether default is probable. The probable/estimable criteria from ASC 450 apply to estimating any contingent loss component, but the stand-ready obligation must be recognized at fair value at inception.
explanations.d: ASC 460-10-30-1 requires guarantors to recognize the fair value of guarantee obligations at inception, even before a default occurs. Fair value reflects the guarantor's stand-ready obligation to perform under the guarantee. For a subsidiary loan guarantee, the parent records: Debit Investment in Subsidiary (or guarantee premium/expense); Credit Guarantee Obligation at fair value. This is a change from prior practice — guarantors can no longer wait for the guaranteed party to default before recognizing any obligation.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company has a take-or-pay contract requiring it to purchase 100,000 units at $10 per unit over the next three years, or pay a penalty of $500,000. Due to a change in business conditions, the company will not use the units and will pay the penalty. How should this commitment be reported at year-end?

answers.text: No recognition — purchase commitments are always off-balance-sheet
Disclose the commitment in footnotes only — the penalty is not yet due
Accrue the full contract value of $1,000,000 — the entire purchase commitment must be expensed when the decision to exit is made
Accrue the $500,000 loss if the decision to pay the penalty is firm and the obligation is probable and estimable — the minimum loss under the contract should be recognized

explanations.a: When a loss on a purchase commitment becomes probable and estimable, it must be accrued — it is not merely a disclosure item.
explanations.b: When the loss is probable and estimable, footnote disclosure alone is insufficient — accrual is required under ASC 450.
explanations.c: The minimum loss ($500,000 penalty) is accrued — not the full contract value ($1,000,000). If the company had to take delivery of goods worth less than $1,000,000, the impairment would be measured as the excess of the contract price over the market price of the goods, which could approach $1,000,000 under different circumstances.
explanations.d: When it is probable that a purchase commitment will result in a loss (either by taking delivery of goods worth less than the contract price, or by paying a penalty to exit), the minimum probable loss is accrued. Here, the company will pay $500,000 rather than honor the $1,000,000 contract — the $500,000 penalty is the minimum loss under the contract and should be accrued when the decision is firm and payment is probable: Debit Loss on Purchase Commitment $500,000; Credit Accrued Liability $500,000.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company estimates environmental remediation costs with a range of $2,000,000 to $5,000,000. All amounts in the range are equally probable. No single amount within the range is a better estimate than any other. Under ASC 450, what amount should be accrued?

answers.text: $5,000,000 — the maximum possible amount reflecting maximum conservatism
$3,500,000 — the midpoint of the range (expected value)
Nothing — without a single best estimate, no accrual is required
$2,000,000 — the minimum in the range when no amount is more likely than others

explanations.a: ASC 450 does not require accruing the maximum amount in a range. The maximum reflects a worst-case scenario, not the standard for accrual.
explanations.b: The midpoint (expected value) approach is used under ASC 450-20-30-1 ONLY when a loss is probable and the amount can only be estimated within a range AND a particular amount within the range is a better estimate than any other. When no amount within the range is a better estimate, the minimum of the range is used.
explanations.c: The contingency meets both accrual criteria (probable and estimable — there is a range of estimates). No accrual would violate ASC 450.
explanations.d: ASC 450-20-30-1 specifies: when the best estimate is a range of equally probable outcomes (no single amount within the range is a better estimate than any other), the minimum amount in the range is accrued. Here: accrue $2,000,000. The difference between the minimum ($2,000,000) and maximum ($5,000,000) is disclosed in the notes as additional possible exposure. This approach may seem conservative in the opposite direction, but it reflects GAAP's specific guidance when the expected-value approach cannot identify a better estimate within the range.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company's management receives a letter of audit inquiry response from outside counsel on January 15 (after the December 31 year-end but before the February 10 financial statement issuance). The letter indicates that a pending lawsuit, previously considered only reasonably possible of loss, is now probable and the estimated loss is $600,000. How should this be treated?

answers.text: Accrue $600,000 in the December 31 financial statements — the change from reasonably possible to probable occurred due to conditions existing at December 31 (the underlying facts were known but the assessment evolved)
No effect on the December 31 financial statements — the new information arose after year-end
Disclose the $600,000 as a Type II subsequent event (non-recognized) in the notes only
Record the $600,000 in Q1 of the next year — the loss is recorded when legal counsel's letter is received

explanations.a: Under ASC 855 (Subsequent Events), events occurring between the balance sheet date and statement issuance date that provide additional evidence about conditions existing at the balance sheet date are 'recognized subsequent events' (Type I) — they must be reflected in the financial statements. The lawsuit existed at December 31; the attorney's updated assessment provides new evidence about the probability of the loss as of December 31. The $600,000 is accrued in the December 31 financial statements even though the letter arrived in January.
explanations.b: Information received between year-end and statement issuance must be considered. If the conditions leading to the reassessment existed at December 31, the financial statements must reflect the updated information.
explanations.c: Type II (non-recognized) subsequent events arise from conditions that did not exist at December 31. Since the lawsuit was pending at year-end (the conditions existed), this is Type I — requiring recognition, not just disclosure.
explanations.d: Recording in Q1 of next year ignores that the underlying condition (the lawsuit and its probable outcome) existed at December 31. The financial statements must reflect available information about year-end conditions.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A retailer offers a two-year product warranty and estimates total warranty costs of $1,500,000 based on 5% of current-year sales of $30,000,000. Actual warranty claims paid during the year totaled $400,000. The beginning warranty liability was $250,000. What is the ending warranty liability?

answers.text: $400,000 — equal to claims paid during the year

explanations.a: Warranty liability rollforward: Beginning balance $250,000; plus: warranty expense accrued = 5% × $30,000,000 = $1,500,000; less: claims paid ($400,000); equals Ending balance = $250,000 + $1,500,000 − $400,000 = $1,350,000. The warranty expense is recognized in the period of sale (matching principle); claims paid reduce the liability when settled. The ending balance represents the estimated future cost of fulfilling warranty obligations on products sold.
explanations.b: This calculation omits the beginning balance. The beginning liability carried forward from prior periods must be included in the rollforward.
explanations.c: The ending liability equals the cumulative estimated future obligations — not just the current-year claims paid.
explanations.d: This calculation omits the reduction for claims paid. Paying warranty claims reduces the accrued liability.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: Under ASC 606, the core principle is that revenue is recognized to depict

answers.text: The transfer of promised goods or services to customers in an amount that reflects the consideration to which the entity expects to be entitled in exchange for those goods or services
Cash collected from customers in the period received — revenue equals cash receipts
Billings to customers in the period invoiced — revenue equals amounts invoiced regardless of delivery
Costs incurred to deliver goods and services plus a reasonable profit margin

explanations.a: ASC 606-10-10-2 states: 'An entity shall recognize revenue to depict the transfer of promised goods or services to customers in an amount that reflects the consideration to which the entity expects to be entitled in exchange for those goods or services.' This principle drives the five-step revenue recognition model: (1) identify the contract; (2) identify performance obligations; (3) determine the transaction price; (4) allocate the transaction price; (5) recognize revenue when (or as) performance obligations are satisfied.
explanations.b: Cash basis revenue recognition does not depict the transfer of goods and services — it reports cash flows, not economic performance. ASC 606 uses accrual-basis principles.
explanations.c: Billing (invoicing) is a separate business process from performance obligation satisfaction. Revenue is recognized when performance obligations are satisfied — not when invoiced.
explanations.d: Cost-plus pricing describes a transaction pricing approach, not the recognition principle. Revenue reflects the consideration the entity is entitled to receive — not costs plus markup.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A software company sells a bundle: software license ($600 standalone selling price) plus 2 years of technical support ($400 standalone selling price). Total contract price is $900. How is the $900 allocated between the two performance obligations?

answers.text: Software license: $900; support: $0 — the entire price is allocated to the most significant deliverable
Software license: $450; support: $450 — split equally between the two elements
Software license: $500; support: $400 — the support receives its full standalone price and the residual goes to the license
Software license: $540; support: $360 — allocated based on relative standalone selling prices: license = $900 × ($600/$1,000); support = $900 × ($400/$1,000)

explanations.a: All of the transaction price cannot be assigned to one element when multiple distinct performance obligations exist. Each obligation receives an allocation.
explanations.b: Equal splitting ignores the relative standalone selling prices, which is the required allocation basis.
explanations.c: The residual approach assigns the remaining amount to a performance obligation only when its SSP is highly variable or uncertain — not as a default. Here, both SSPs are known, so relative SSP allocation applies.
explanations.d: ASC 606-10-32-31 requires allocating the transaction price based on relative standalone selling prices. License SSP = $600; Support SSP = $400; Total SSP = $1,000. License allocation = $900 × ($600/$1,000) = $540. Support allocation = $900 × ($400/$1,000) = $360. Total = $900 ✓. Revenue is recognized: $540 at license delivery (point in time) and $360 over the 2-year support period (over time).

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A contractor enters into a $10,000,000 long-term construction contract. At year-end, costs incurred are $3,000,000 and estimated costs to complete are $5,000,000 (total estimated cost = $8,000,000). Using the percentage-of-completion method (cost-to-cost), what revenue is recognized in the current year?

answers.text: $10,000,000 — all revenue is recognized when the contract is signed
$3,000,000 — revenue equals costs incurred
$5,000,000 — revenue is split evenly over two years

explanations.a: Revenue is recognized as the performance obligation is satisfied over time — not at contract inception.
explanations.b: Revenue does not simply equal costs incurred — the percentage complete determines the revenue recognized, which reflects the profit margin as well.
explanations.c: Cost-to-cost percentage of completion: Percentage complete = Costs incurred to date / Total estimated costs = $3,000,000 / $8,000,000 = 37.5%. Revenue recognized = 37.5% × $10,000,000 = $3,750,000. Gross profit recognized = $3,750,000 − $3,000,000 = $750,000. This method satisfies ASC 606's 'over time' recognition when the customer controls the asset as it is created or enhanced, and the contractor's performance does not create an asset with alternative use.
explanations.d: Revenue is not split evenly unless costs are incurred evenly over the project. The cost-to-cost method measures actual progress based on costs, not time elapsed.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company sells goods with a right of return. Historical data shows 5% of goods are returned. The company sells 10,000 units at $50 each ($500,000 total). Under ASC 606, how should the transaction be recorded at the time of sale?

answers.text: Revenue = $475,000 (expected net sales of 9,500 units × $50); Refund Liability = $25,000; Return Asset = cost of 500 expected returned units
Revenue = $500,000; no adjustments — returns are recorded only when received
Revenue = $0 — contracts with return rights cannot recognize revenue until the return period expires
Revenue = $475,000; cost of goods sold is not adjusted for expected returns

explanations.a: Under ASC 606-10-55-22, when rights of return exist: Revenue is recognized only for the goods expected to be retained by customers = (10,000 − 500 expected returns) × $50 = $475,000. A refund liability of $25,000 is recorded for expected returns. A return asset is recorded for the expected cost of goods to be returned (the inventory that will come back). When returns actually occur: Refund Liability is reduced, cash is refunded, and the return asset is converted to inventory. This presentation reflects the variable consideration guidance — only include amounts it is highly probable will not reverse.
explanations.b: Variable consideration (expected returns) must be estimated and constrained under ASC 606. Recording full revenue ignores the probable returns.
explanations.c: Rights of return do not prevent revenue recognition — they require adjusting the transaction price for expected returns.
explanations.d: Both revenue and cost of goods sold must be adjusted for expected returns. The cost of goods associated with expected returns is not expensed — it becomes a return asset.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A travel agency books airline tickets on behalf of customers and earns a 10% commission. The agency collects the full ticket price from customers ($1,000 per ticket) and remits 90% to the airline. Acting as an agent (not a principal), what revenue does the agency recognize per ticket?

answers.text: $1,000 — the agency collected the full amount from the customer
$900 — the amount remitted to the airline
$100 — the net commission earned as agent; the $1,000 collected is not the agency's revenue because it does not control the service before it is transferred to the customer
$0 — agents cannot recognize any revenue until the airline performs

explanations.a: Gross revenue recognition ($1,000) applies to principals who control the service before it is transferred. The agency does not control the airline seat — it merely facilitates the transaction.
explanations.b: $900 is the amount remitted to the airline — not the agency's revenue. The remittance is a payment to the service provider, not revenue.
explanations.c: Under ASC 606-10-55-36, an entity is an agent when it does not control the specified good or service before it is transferred. Indicators of agency include: another party is primarily responsible for fulfillment; inventory risk is with another party; limited discretion in setting price. The travel agency is an agent: the airline controls and provides the service. Agent revenue = net fee earned = $1,000 × 10% = $100 per ticket. The $900 is collected and remitted as a pass-through — not revenue.
explanations.d: Agents do recognize revenue — but only their net commission, recognized when the agency service is complete (the ticket is booked and the customer obtains the right to travel).

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A customer pays $1,200 at contract inception for a 12-month magazine subscription starting March 1. The company's fiscal year ends December 31. How much revenue is recognized in the first fiscal year and how much is deferred?

answers.text: $100 per month; $1,000 recognized (10 months: March–December); $200 deferred (January–February of next year)
$1,200 recognized at contract inception — prepayment triggers immediate recognition
$600 recognized (6 months); $600 deferred (6 months)
$0 recognized; $1,200 deferred until all 12 monthly magazines are delivered

explanations.a: Performance obligations are satisfied over time as each monthly magazine is delivered. Monthly revenue = $1,200 / 12 = $100. In the first fiscal year (March 1 through December 31 = 10 months): Revenue recognized = 10 × $100 = $1,000. Deferred revenue at December 31 = 2 months × $100 = $200 (for January and February issues). The deferred revenue is a current liability since the remaining performance obligations will be satisfied within 12 months.
explanations.b: Revenue is recognized as magazines are delivered (over time) — not when the subscription fee is received. Receipt of cash creates a contract liability (deferred revenue), not immediate revenue.
explanations.c: 6 months would apply only if the subscription started July 1. With a March 1 start, 10 months fall in the current fiscal year.
explanations.d: Waiting until all 12 magazines are delivered to recognize any revenue ignores the over-time recognition pattern. Each monthly delivery satisfies a portion of the performance obligation.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A construction company has a long-term contract with total estimated costs of $6,000,000 and contract price of $8,000,000. At year-end, costs incurred are $4,500,000 and the estimate to complete has increased to $3,000,000 (total now = $7,500,000). What is the impact on current-year income?

answers.text: Revenue based on percent complete under new total estimate; loss accrued if total estimated costs exceed contract price
Revenue of $6,000,000 and profit of $500,000 — based on the original estimated profit
No recognition — cost overruns require stopping all revenue recognition until the revised estimate is finalized
Revenue of $4,500,000 and zero profit — cost overruns eliminate profit on a contract-by-contract basis

explanations.a: When total estimated costs increase: New total estimated costs = $7,500,000; Contract price = $8,000,000; Estimated total profit = $500,000. Percentage complete = $4,500,000 / $7,500,000 = 60%. Cumulative revenue to date = 60% × $8,000,000 = $4,800,000. If $3,000,000 was recognized in prior periods (based on then-current estimates), current-year revenue = $4,800,000 − prior recognition. The income statement reflects the revised margin. Crucially: if total estimated costs ($7,500,000) EXCEEDED the contract price ($8,000,000), a loss would be recognized immediately (full expected loss accrued in the current period under ASC 606).
explanations.b: The revised estimate changes the percentage complete and the expected total margin. Using the original estimate ignores the cost overrun information.
explanations.c: Revenue recognition continues on cost-overrun contracts — the percentage complete is recalculated using the new total estimate. Only if a loss is expected on the overall contract is recognition altered.
explanations.d: Revenue equals the percentage complete times total contract price — not simply costs incurred. Gross profit (positive or negative) is recognized as work progresses.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A customer pays a $50,000 nonrefundable upfront fee to initiate a service contract. The fee does not relate to the transfer of a distinct good or service — it relates to setup activities that are an administrative necessity. Under ASC 606, how is the fee treated?

answers.text: Recognized immediately as revenue — nonrefundable fees are always recognized at receipt
Expensed by the customer and recognized by the service provider at contract termination
Recognized as OCI and reclassified to revenue when the service contract ends

Recognized as a contract liability and allocated to the performance obligation(s) in the contract — the fee is part of the transaction price but relates to future service delivery, not a distinct deliverable

explanations.a: Nonrefundable upfront fees are not automatically recognized at receipt. ASC 606 evaluates whether the fee relates to the transfer of a distinct good or service. If it does not, it is deferred and allocated to the ongoing service obligation.
explanations.b: Recognition is not deferred until contract termination. Revenue is recognized as service is provided over the contract term.
explanations.c: Contract liabilities flow to revenue — not OCI — as performance obligations are satisfied. OCI is not used for deferred revenue from service contracts.
explanations.d: Under ASC 606-10-55-51, nonrefundable upfront fees must be evaluated to determine whether they are payment for a distinct good or service. Setup activities that are administrative necessities do not transfer a distinct good or service to the customer — they represent fulfillment activities. Therefore: the $50,000 is a contract liability at receipt; it is allocated to the service performance obligation and recognized over the service period as services are delivered. The customer is effectively prepaying for the ongoing service, not for a separate distinct deliverable.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A deferred tax liability (DTL) arises when

answers.text: A company's taxable income exceeds book income in the current year — higher taxes now create a future asset
A company records a net operating loss carryforward — losses carried forward are deferred tax liabilities
A company records a permanent difference that reduces book income but not taxable income
A temporary difference causes a company to pay less tax currently than it will owe in future periods — the future tax payment obligation is a deferred tax liability

explanations.a: When taxable income exceeds book income currently, more taxes are paid now than the book income warrants — this creates a deferred tax ASSET (prepaid taxes), not a liability.
explanations.b: Net operating loss carryforwards (NOLs) create deferred tax ASSETS — they represent future tax benefits that will reduce future taxable income. DTLs arise from excess taxable income in the future, not from NOLs.
explanations.c: Permanent differences (e.g., tax-exempt interest, non-deductible fines) affect the current tax provision but do not create deferred tax assets or liabilities — they have no future tax consequence because they never reverse.
explanations.d: A DTL arises when a temporary difference causes the tax basis of an asset or liability to differ from its book basis in a way that will result in taxable amounts in future periods. The most common example: accelerated tax depreciation reduces taxable income now but will result in higher taxable income later when book depreciation exceeds tax depreciation. The future tax payments represent the DTL recorded today: DTL = Taxable temporary difference × Enacted future tax rate.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company has book income before taxes of $500,000. Permanent differences include $30,000 of tax-exempt municipal bond interest (reduces taxable income) and $20,000 of non-deductible fines (increases taxable income). The tax rate is 25%. What is the current income tax expense?

answers.text: $125,000 — 25% × $500,000 (permanent differences are ignored in tax expense)

explanations.a: Permanent differences DO affect taxable income and current tax expense — they just don't create deferred taxes. Ignoring them overstates or understates tax expense.
explanations.b: This produces $122,500 = 25% × $490,000, which is actually the same calculation as option d — both arrive at the correct answer through the same math.
explanations.c: $127,500 = 25% × $510,000 — this incorrectly adds the fine and subtracts the municipal interest in opposite directions.
explanations.d: Taxable income = Book income +/- permanent differences: $500,000 − $30,000 (municipal interest is tax-exempt, so excluded from taxable income) + $20,000 (fines non-deductible for tax, so added back to taxable income) = $490,000. Current income tax expense = $490,000 × 25% = $122,500. The effective tax rate = $122,500 / $500,000 = 24.5% (different from 25% statutory rate because of permanent differences).

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company uses straight-line depreciation for book purposes ($50,000 per year) and MACRS for tax purposes ($80,000 in Year 1). In Year 1, what deferred tax account is created, assuming a 21% tax rate?

answers.text: Deferred tax asset of $6,300 — excess book depreciation over tax creates a future benefit
Deferred tax asset of $10,080 — the full MACRS deduction times 21%
No deferred tax — depreciation differences are permanent differences
Deferred tax liability of $6,300 — MACRS depreciation ($80,000) exceeds book depreciation ($50,000) by $30,000; the taxable temporary difference × 21% = $6,300

explanations.a: When tax depreciation exceeds book depreciation in early years, taxable income is lower than book income — taxes are deferred to future years. This is a DTL, not a DTA.
explanations.b: The DTA/DTL is based on the DIFFERENCE between tax and book depreciation ($30,000) — not the full MACRS amount ($80,000).
explanations.c: Depreciation method differences are classic temporary differences (they reverse over the asset's life) — not permanent differences. Permanent differences never reverse.
explanations.d: Taxable temporary difference = Tax depreciation − Book depreciation = $80,000 − $50,000 = $30,000. Because the tax deduction ($80,000) exceeds the book expense ($50,000), the company pays less tax currently but will owe more in future years (when MACRS deductions are exhausted but book depreciation continues). DTL = $30,000 × 21% = $6,300. Journal: Debit Income Tax Expense $6,300; Credit Deferred Tax Liability $6,300 (as part of total deferred tax provision). The DTL reverses in later years as MACRS deductions fall below straight-line book depreciation.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company has a $400,000 net operating loss (NOL) carryforward and a 25% tax rate. Management concludes it is more likely than not that $250,000 of the NOL will be utilized. What are the deferred tax asset and valuation allowance?

answers.text: DTA = $100,000; Valuation allowance = $0 — the full NOL creates a DTA with no allowance needed
DTA = $100,000; Valuation allowance = $37,500 — based on the uncertain portion
DTA = $100,000 gross; Valuation allowance = $37,500 (25% × $150,000 uncertain portion) — net DTA = $62,500
DTA = $0 — NOL carryforwards do not create deferred tax assets

explanations.a: A valuation allowance is required when it is more likely than not that some portion of the DTA will not be realized. Here, $150,000 of the NOL is not expected to be used — a valuation allowance is required.
explanations.b: The gross DTA = $400,000 × 25% = $100,000. Valuation allowance = uncertain portion × rate = $150,000 × 25% = $37,500. Net DTA = $100,000 − $37,500 = $62,500.
explanations.c: Gross DTA = $400,000 NOL × 25% = $100,000. Management expects only $250,000 to be utilized; $150,000 is uncertain. Valuation allowance = $150,000 × 25% = $37,500 (the portion of the DTA not expected to be realized). Net DTA recognized = $100,000 − $37,500 = $62,500. Journal: Debit DTA $100,000; Credit Income Tax Benefit $100,000; then Debit Income Tax Expense $37,500; Credit Valuation Allowance $37,500. Net benefit = $62,500 recognized.
explanations.d: NOL carryforwards are a primary source of deferred tax assets — they represent future tax deductions that reduce taxable income in future years.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: Congress enacts a tax rate increase from 21% to 28% effective next year. A company has existing deferred tax liabilities of $210,000 (computed at 21%). What adjustment is made in the current year?

answers.text: No adjustment — deferred taxes are adjusted only when they reverse
DTL increases by $70,000 to $280,000; income tax expense increases by $70,000 — the enacted rate change requires remeasuring all deferred tax balances in the period of enactment
DTL decreases by $70,000 — higher tax rates reduce the future tax benefit
DTL increases; the $70,000 adjustment goes to OCI — rate change effects on deferred taxes are OCI items

explanations.a: ASC 740 requires remeasuring deferred tax balances when a tax rate change is enacted — not when it becomes effective or when temporary differences reverse.
explanations.b: ASC 740-10-35-4 requires that deferred tax assets and liabilities be adjusted for the effect of an enacted change in tax rates in the period of enactment (when the legislation is signed into law). New DTL = $210,000 / 21% × 28% = $280,000. Adjustment = $280,000 − $210,000 = $70,000. This $70,000 is recorded as additional income tax expense in the period of enactment: Debit Income Tax Expense $70,000; Credit Deferred Tax Liability $70,000. The company now recognizes that its future tax payments will be larger than previously estimated due to the higher rate.
explanations.c: A higher future tax rate means MORE taxes will be paid when temporary differences reverse — the DTL increases, not decreases.
explanations.d: Tax rate change adjustments to deferred tax balances flow through income tax expense (in the income statement) — not OCI. Only specific items (like AOCI-related deferred taxes) use OCI.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company has book income of $500,000. The only book-tax differences are: MACRS depreciation exceeds straight-line by $80,000 (taxable temp. diff.); warranty accrual recognized for book but not deductible for tax: $40,000 (deductible temp. diff.); tax-exempt interest: $10,000 (permanent). Tax rate = 25%. What is total income tax expense?

answers.text: $122,500 — 25% × ($500,000 − $10,000) book income excluding perm. diff.
$117,500 — current $107,500 + deferred $10,000 net

explanations.a: $122,500 is the correct total income tax expense, but option d provides the full breakdown showing current vs. deferred components.
explanations.b: Taxable income = $500,000 book − $80,000 extra MACRS + $40,000 warranty not deductible − $10,000 tax-exempt = $450,000. Current tax = $450,000 × 25% = $112,500. This option's path contains an arithmetic error.
explanations.c: $117,500 does not reconcile to the correct calculation. Total income tax expense = book income (net of permanent diffs) × rate = ($500,000 − $10,000) × 25% = $122,500.
explanations.d: Total income tax expense = (Book income − Permanent differences) × Rate = ($500,000 − $10,000) × 25% = $122,500. Current tax = Taxable income × Rate: taxable income = $500,000 − $80,000 (MACRS) + $40,000 (warranty) − $10,000 (exempt) = $450,000; current = $450,000 × 25% = $112,500. Net deferred tax expense = $122,500 − $112,500 = $10,000 (DTL for depreciation $80,000 × 25% = $20,000 minus DTA for warranty $40,000 × 25% = $10,000 = net $10,000 deferred expense). Journal: Debit Tax Expense $122,500; Credit Tax Payable $112,500; Credit Net Deferred Tax $10,000.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company reports book income of $600,000. The only difference between book and taxable income is accelerated tax depreciation of $100,000 (tax depreciation exceeds book depreciation by $100,000). The tax rate is 25%. What are: (1) taxable income, (2) current tax payable, (3) deferred tax liability change, and (4) total income tax expense?

explanations.a: Options a and c produce identical numbers — option c includes the additional explanation showing the total income tax expense check.
explanations.b: When tax depreciation exceeds book depreciation, taxable income is LOWER (not higher) than book income — $500,000, not $700,000.
explanations.c: Step-by-step: (1) Taxable income = $600,000 book income − $100,000 extra tax depreciation = $500,000; (2) Current tax payable = $500,000 × 25% = $125,000; (3) Deferred tax liability increases = $100,000 temporary difference × 25% = $25,000 (future taxable amounts when book depreciation > tax depreciation in later years); (4) Total income tax expense = Current ($125,000) + Deferred ($25,000) = $150,000 = $600,000 × 25% ✓. Journal: Debit Income Tax Expense $150,000; Credit Income Tax Payable $125,000; Credit DTL $25,000.
explanations.d: There IS a deferred tax when taxable income differs from book income due to a temporary difference. The accelerated depreciation creates a taxable temporary difference that must be recognized as a DTL.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: Which of the following creates a deferred tax ASSET (DTA)?

answers.text: MACRS accelerated depreciation exceeding straight-line book depreciation in early years
Installment sale revenue recognized for tax purposes when collected but fully recognized for book purposes at point of sale
Warranty expense accrued for book purposes but deductible for tax only when paid — creating a deductible temporary difference
Percentage depletion for tax in excess of cost depletion for book

explanations.a: MACRS in excess of book depreciation creates a DTL (taxable temporary difference) — tax deductions are taken now; higher future taxable income will result. This increases future tax payments.
explanations.b: Installment sales recognized for tax when collected but for book at point of sale means: book income is higher than taxable income now (tax is deferred). This creates a DTL — more taxes will be owed in the future when collections occur.
explanations.c: Warranty accruals create a DTA. Book expense = $X now (matching principle); Tax deduction = $X later (when claims are actually paid). Tax basis of warranty liability = $0 (not yet deductible); book basis = $X (liability recognized). This deductible temporary difference means: the company will deduct warranty costs for tax purposes in future periods — reducing future taxable income — which is a future tax benefit. DTA = Warranty liability balance × Tax rate.
explanations.d: Percentage depletion exceeding cost depletion for tax purposes is generally a permanent difference (the excess over cost depletion has no book counterpart) — it does not create a deferred tax item.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: Under ASC 820, fair value is defined as

answers.text: The historical cost of an asset or liability as recorded when originally acquired
The exit price — the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date
The replacement cost — the amount it would cost to replace the asset with a new equivalent
The net realizable value — the expected cash inflows less costs of completion and disposal

explanations.a: Historical cost is a measurement attribute — not the definition of fair value. Historical cost reflects what was paid, not what the asset is worth today.
explanations.b: ASC 820-10-20 defines fair value as 'the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date.' Key features: (1) Exit price — what sellers receive (not entry price paid); (2) Orderly transaction — not a forced sale or distressed liquidation; (3) Market participants — hypothetical willing buyer and seller, knowledgeable and able; (4) At the measurement date — current market conditions.
explanations.c: Replacement cost is an entry price — what it costs to replace an asset. Fair value is an exit price (selling price) — these differ for many assets. Replacement cost is used in certain GAAP contexts but is not the definition of fair value.
explanations.d: Net realizable value is used for inventory measurement under ASC 330 — not the definition of fair value under ASC 820. NRV reflects a selling price less disposal costs for a specific purpose; fair value is broader.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company's machine has a book value of $80,000. The machine cost $200,000 when new. Identical machines sell for $65,000 in used equipment markets. The machine could be replaced with a new one for $220,000. What is the fair value under ASC 820?

answers.text: $220,000 — replacement cost is the fair value of productive assets
$80,000 — book value represents fair value under the asset approach
$200,000 — original cost is fair value for non-financial assets
$65,000 — the price that would be received to sell the asset to a market participant in an orderly transaction

explanations.a: Replacement cost ($220,000) is an entry price — what it costs to acquire an equivalent new asset. ASC 820 uses the exit price (selling price), not the entry price.
explanations.b: Book value ($80,000) reflects historical cost minus accumulated depreciation — it is an accounting construct, not a market-based exit price.
explanations.c: Original cost ($200,000) is the entry price paid at acquisition — not the current exit price. Markets have moved since purchase.
explanations.d: ASC 820 defines fair value as an exit price — the price that would be received to SELL the asset. The used equipment market price of $65,000 represents what market participants would pay for this machine in an orderly transaction. This is the fair value, even though it is less than book value or replacement cost.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company measures a financial liability at fair value. The company's own credit risk has deteriorated since issuance, reducing the fair value of the liability from $1,000,000 to $900,000. Under ASC 820, how is the $100,000 fair value change from the credit deterioration recorded?

answers.text: Recognized as a $100,000 gain in net income — the liability decreased in value
No recognition — changes in an entity's own credit risk are not recognized under GAAP

Recognized as a $100,000 gain in other comprehensive income (OCI) — changes in fair value of liabilities due to instrument-specific credit risk are reported in OCI when the fair value option is elected
Recognized as a $100,000 loss in net income — credit deterioration always increases expense

explanations.a: The counterintuitive gain from credit deterioration (liability decreases = gain) is recognized — but in OCI, not net income, for the credit risk portion.
explanations.b: Changes in fair value due to own credit risk ARE recognized — but in OCI rather than net income under the fair value option.
explanations.c: ASC 825-10-45-5 requires that for financial liabilities carried at fair value under the fair value option, the portion of fair value change attributable to instrument-specific credit risk (the entity's own credit deterioration) be reported in OCI rather than net income. This prevents the counterintuitive income statement result where credit deterioration (a negative event) produces a gain. The remaining fair value change (e.g., from interest rate movements) flows through net income.
explanations.d: Credit deterioration decreases the fair value of the liability (lower fair value = smaller obligation). This is economically a gain for the debtor — not a loss. Under ASC 820, a liability's fair value reflects the amount needed to transfer the obligation to a market participant.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the income approach to fair value measurement under ASC 820?

answers.text: Values an asset based on the cost to replace or reproduce it, adjusted for obsolescence
Values an asset based on comparable market transactions for similar assets
Values an asset or liability by converting future cash flows or income to a present value amount — using discount rates that reflect market participant assumptions
Values an asset based on the most recent price at which the entity acquired it

explanations.a: Valuing an asset based on cost to replace or reproduce (adjusted for obsolescence) describes the cost approach — not the income approach.
explanations.b: Valuing based on comparable market transactions describes the market approach — using prices and other relevant information from market transactions involving identical or comparable assets.
explanations.c: The income approach (ASC 820-10-55-3) converts future amounts (cash flows, income, or expenses) to a single current (discounted) amount. Techniques include: discounted cash flow (DCF) analysis; option pricing models; and multi-period excess earnings method. The discount rate reflects market participant assumptions about risk, time value, and the specific characteristics of the asset/liability. This approach is common for intangible assets, reporting units, and complex financial instruments.
explanations.d: Recent acquisition price is a historical entry price — not a forward-looking approach. It may be relevant evidence of fair value in some cases but does not define the income approach.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company must determine the fair value of a unique manufacturing facility. There are no comparable sales of identical or similar facilities. However, the facility generates identifiable cash flows that can be projected and discounted. What valuation approach is most appropriate, and at what hierarchy level would this fair value likely be classified?

answers.text: Market approach at Level 1 — all real estate has quoted prices
Cost approach at Level 2 — replacement cost uses observable inputs
Income approach (DCF) at Level 3 — unobservable inputs (management's projected cash flows and discount rate) are used when comparable market transactions are unavailable
Income approach at Level 1 — cash flow projections are publicly available for manufacturers

explanations.a: No active market exists for unique manufacturing facilities — Level 1 (quoted prices in active markets for identical assets) is not available.
explanations.b: The cost approach (replacement cost minus obsolescence) uses estimates that are largely unobservable, not observable market inputs. This would typically be Level 3, not Level 2.
explanations.c: For a unique asset with no comparable market transactions, the income approach (DCF) is often most appropriate — converting the facility's expected future cash flows to a present value. Since the key inputs (projected revenues, operating costs, growth rates, and discount rate) are management's own estimates without corroboration from observable market data, the resulting fair value measurement is Level 3. Level 3 is appropriate when significant unobservable inputs are required because observable market information is not available for the specific asset.
explanations.d: Cash flow projections for private manufacturing facilities are not publicly available — they are entity-specific, unobservable inputs, making the measurement Level 3.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: When measuring fair value for a financial asset that trades in multiple markets, ASC 820 requires using the price in which market?

answers.text: The market with the highest price — maximizing reported asset values
The market where the entity usually trades — regardless of prices in other markets
The principal market — the market with the greatest volume and level of activity; or, if no principal market exists, the most advantageous market (highest net price after transaction costs)
The domestic market — international market prices are excluded from US GAAP fair value measurements

explanations.a: The highest-price market is only relevant if it is the most advantageous market AND no principal market exists — highest price alone does not determine which market to use.
explanations.b: The entity's usual trading venue is relevant evidence for identifying the principal market, but the principal market is defined by volume and activity — not by the entity's habits.
explanations.c: ASC 820-10-25-6 establishes a market priority hierarchy: (1) Principal market — the market with the greatest volume and level of activity for the asset/liability. The fair value is the price in the principal market (even if a different market offers a higher price); (2) If no principal market exists — the most advantageous market: the market that maximizes the amount received after transaction costs (net proceeds). Note: transaction costs are not deducted from the fair value measurement itself — they affect which market is most advantageous but fair value equals the unadjusted price (before transaction costs).
explanations.d: There is no restriction limiting fair value to domestic markets. Global markets are considered, and the principal or most advantageous market may be international.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company holds an investment in a private equity fund measured using net asset value (NAV) as a practical expedient under ASC 820. The NAV is $5,000,000. The company cannot redeem this investment for 18 months. Under the NAV practical expedient, at what hierarchy level is this investment classified?

answers.text: Level 1 — NAV is an observable market price
Level 2 — NAV is a market-corroborated observable input
Level 3 — all private equity investments are Level 3 regardless of NAV availability
Not categorized within the fair value hierarchy — investments measured using the NAV practical expedient are excluded from the Level 1, 2, and 3 hierarchy categorization

explanations.a: NAV is not a quoted price in an active market for the fund itself — it is an accounting-based measure computed by the fund manager. Level 1 requires quoted prices for identical assets in active markets.
explanations.b: NAV does not meet the criteria for Level 2 (observable inputs other than Level 1). It is computed internally by the fund based on the underlying investments' fair values.
explanations.c: While private equity is often Level 3, investments measured using the NAV practical expedient are specifically excluded from hierarchy categorization altogether.
explanations.d: ASC 820-10-15-5 permits entities to use NAV as a practical expedient to estimate fair value when NAV is computed consistent with ASC 946 and the entity can redeem at NAV (or within a near-term period). Importantly, investments measured using the NAV practical expedient are NOT categorized within the Level 1, 2, or 3 hierarchy — they are disclosed separately. This exclusion applies regardless of whether redemption is currently possible (even with the 18-month lock-up, the practical expedient and hierarchy exclusion still apply if NAV is the basis).

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: Under ASC 842, which of the following is correct about operating leases for lessees?

answers.text: Operating leases are kept off the balance sheet — only finance leases are recognized as assets and liabilities
Operating leases create both a right-of-use (ROU) asset and a lease liability on the balance sheet; lease cost is recognized as a single straight-line expense over the lease term
Operating leases are recognized only in the income statement as rent expense — no balance sheet impact
Operating leases are always classified as finance leases under ASC 842 — the two categories were merged

explanations.a: Under ASC 842, ALL leases with terms greater than 12 months must be recognized on the balance sheet — including operating leases. The old 'off-balance-sheet' treatment for operating leases was eliminated.
explanations.b: ASC 842 requires lessees to recognize: (1) A right-of-use (ROU) asset representing the right to use the underlying asset; (2) A lease liability representing the obligation to make lease payments. Both are recognized for operating AND finance leases. For operating leases, the income statement shows a single straight-line lease cost (blending interest and amortization into one line), which differs from finance leases (separate interest expense and amortization). The balance sheet impact is the major change from prior GAAP.
explanations.c: The balance sheet impact is a central feature of ASC 842 — operating leases now appear on the balance sheet, unlike under the old ASC 840.
explanations.d: ASC 842 maintains the distinction between operating leases and finance leases — they are separate categories with different income statement presentation. They were not merged.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A lessee signs a 5-year operating lease with annual payments of $24,000 (paid at year-end). The lessee's incremental borrowing rate is 6%. The present value of 5 annual payments of $24,000 at 6% is $101,092. What is recorded at lease commencement?

answers.text: Debit ROU Asset $120,000; Credit Lease Liability $120,000 — undiscounted payments
No entry — operating leases are not on the balance sheet
Debit ROU Asset $101,092; Credit Lease Liability $101,092 — present value of lease payments
Debit Prepaid Rent $101,092; Credit Cash $101,092 — all lease payments prepaid at inception

explanations.a: The lease liability is measured at the present value of future lease payments — not the undiscounted total. Recording undiscounted payments overstates the liability.
explanations.b: Under ASC 842, operating leases with terms greater than 12 months must be recognized on the balance sheet. There is no off-balance-sheet treatment.
explanations.c: At lease commencement: Debit Right-of-Use Asset $101,092; Credit Lease Liability $101,092. The lease liability = present value of remaining lease payments discounted at the lessee's incremental borrowing rate (or implicit rate if known) = $101,092. The ROU asset initially equals the lease liability (adjusted for lease incentives, initial direct costs, and prepaid/accrued payments). The ROU asset is amortized, and the lease liability is reduced as payments are made (using interest method).
explanations.d: Lease payments are made over time — not prepaid at inception. Prepaid rent is not the appropriate treatment for the initial recognition of a lease under ASC 842.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: Under ASC 842, which criteria, if met, classify a lease as a FINANCE lease (rather than an operating lease)?

answers.text: The lease term exceeds one year — all multi-year leases are finance leases

Title transfers OR lessee has a purchase option likely to be exercised OR lease term is for major part of useful life OR PV of payments equals substantially all of fair value OR asset is specialized with no alternative use to lessor
Only leases of real estate are finance leases — equipment leases are always operating
The lease has a fixed payment schedule — variable payment leases cannot be finance leases

explanations.a: Multi-year alone does not make a lease a finance lease. Finance lease classification requires meeting at least one of five specific criteria.
explanations.b: ASC 842-20-25-2 classifies a lessee's lease as a finance lease if any one of these criteria is met: (1) Transfer of ownership by end of lease term; (2) Purchase option that the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise; (3) Lease term covers the major part of the asset's remaining economic life (typically interpreted as 75%+); (4) Present value of lease payments (including purchase options reasonably certain to be exercised) equals or exceeds substantially all of the fair value of the underlying asset (typically 90%+); (5) Asset is specialized with no alternative use to the lessor at end of the lease. These mirror the old capital lease criteria (with updated thresholds) — any single criterion triggers finance lease classification.
explanations.c: Finance leases can involve any type of asset — real property, equipment, vehicles, aircraft, or others. There is no blanket rule that real estate leases are finance leases.
explanations.d: Variable payments (based on usage or an index) can be included in lease payments and can contribute to meeting the finance lease criteria. Fixed payment structure is not required.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A lessee has a finance lease. The initial lease liability is $200,000 at 8% interest, with a first payment of $50,000 due one year after commencement. What are lease liability and ROU asset after Year 1?

answers.text: Lease liability = $150,000; ROU asset amortized based on lease term
Lease liability = $166,000 ($200,000 × 1.08 − $50,000); ROU asset amortized separately on straight-line basis
Lease liability = $150,000; ROU asset = lease liability
Lease liability = $200,000 (unchanged until final payment); ROU asset amortized

explanations.a: The lease liability does not simply decrease by the payment amount — interest accrues first.
explanations.b: Finance lease Year 1: Interest accrual = $200,000 × 8% = $16,000 added to liability; Payment = $50,000 reducing liability; Ending lease liability = $200,000 + $16,000 − $50,000 = $166,000. Income statement: Interest expense = $16,000; Amortization of ROU asset = separately computed (straight-line over the shorter of lease term or useful life if ownership not transferred). Unlike operating leases (single straight-line cost), finance leases produce front-loaded total expense (higher interest in early years).
explanations.c: For finance leases, the ROU asset is amortized separately from the lease liability using the straight-line method (or another systematic basis). The two balances diverge after commencement.
explanations.d: The lease liability changes each period as interest accrues and payments are made. It does not remain constant until the final payment.
