questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company signs a 10-month office lease. Monthly rent is $5,000. The company elects the short-term lease exemption under ASC 842. How is this lease accounted for?

answers.text: Recognized on the balance sheet with a ROU asset and lease liability — all leases require balance sheet recognition

Recognized as rent expense on a straight-line basis over 10 months; no ROU asset or lease liability on the balance sheet — the short-term lease exemption allows off-balance-sheet treatment for leases with terms of 12 months or less
Capitalized as leasehold improvements and depreciated over 10 months
Recognized as a finance lease since the remaining term is under 1 year

explanations.a: The short-term lease exemption specifically allows lessees to elect off-balance-sheet treatment for qualifying short-term leases.
explanations.b: ASC 842-20-25-2 permits lessees to elect not to apply the recognition requirements for leases with terms of 12 months or less at commencement (after considering renewal options the entity is reasonably certain to exercise). When elected, short-term lease payments are recognized as lease cost on a straight-line basis over the lease term (or another systematic basis). No ROU asset or lease liability is recognized on the balance sheet. The 10-month lease qualifies since the term ≤ 12 months. Monthly expense = $5,000; total lease cost = $50,000 over 10 months.
explanations.c: Lease payments are rent expense — not leasehold improvements. Leasehold improvements are physical alterations to the leased space, not lease payments.
explanations.d: Lease term does not determine finance vs. operating classification — the five criteria in ASC 842-20-25-2 apply. Short-term leases using the exemption bypass the classification criteria altogether.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A lessee has an operating lease with Year 1 payments of $30,000, Year 2 payments of $35,000, and Year 3 payments of $40,000. The PV of all lease payments is $90,000 (initial lease liability and ROU asset). How is Year 1 lease cost calculated under ASC 842?

answers.text: $30,000 — the actual cash payment made in Year 1
$35,000 — one-third of total payments ($105,000 / 3 years)
$35,000 — straight-line lease cost over 3 years = total undiscounted payments ($105,000) / 3 = $35,000 per year
Year 1 interest expense on lease liability plus ROU amortization separately computed

explanations.a: Cash payments are not the lease cost for operating leases — straight-line recognition produces a level cost regardless of variable payment amounts.
explanations.b: Options b and c arrive at the same answer ($35,000) — option c provides the calculation showing it is total undiscounted payments divided by lease term.
explanations.c: Under ASC 842, operating lease cost is recognized on a straight-line basis over the lease term. Total undiscounted lease payments = $30,000 + $35,000 + $40,000 = $105,000. Annual straight-line lease cost = $105,000 / 3 years = $35,000. The difference between the straight-line cost ($35,000) and actual cash payment ($30,000 in Year 1) creates changes in the ROU asset and lease liability. The ROU asset is reduced by the difference between cash paid and interest on the liability (a specific amortization plug that ensures straight-line expense). This differs from finance leases, which separately present interest expense and ROU amortization.
explanations.d: Operating leases do NOT separately present interest and amortization — the single-line straight-line lease cost is the distinguishing feature. Finance leases use the separate interest + amortization presentation described in option d.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A lessee's operating lease expires and the lessee exercises a 3-year renewal option that was not included in the original lease term because it was not reasonably certain to be exercised. Under ASC 842, this is treated as

answers.text: A continuation of the original lease — renewals are automatically part of the original lease term

A lease modification — the lessee remeasures the ROU asset and lease liability to include the additional 3-year period, discounted at the revised lessee's incremental borrowing rate at the modification date
A new lease — the renewal option is treated as a new lease commencement; the entity applies ASC 842 from the beginning of the renewal period
An extension of the original lease reported only in footnotes — no balance sheet change is required until payments increase

explanations.a: Renewal options not included in the original lease term (because not reasonably certain) are not automatically part of the original lease measurement. Exercising them triggers a remeasurement.
explanations.b: Under ASC 842-20-45-3, exercising a renewal option that was not previously included in the lease term is a lease modification. At the modification date, the lessee remeasures the lease liability at the present value of the remaining payments (including the new 3-year renewal period) discounted at the lessee's current incremental borrowing rate. The ROU asset is adjusted by the same amount as the lease liability change. The remeasured amounts are used for subsequent accounting.
explanations.c: Modifications are generally not treated as new leases unless they involve a new right of use not included in the original lease (and meet other criteria). Exercising a renewal option for the same underlying asset is a modification — not a new lease.
explanations.d: Lease modifications require immediate balance sheet adjustment — not merely footnote disclosure.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: Under ASC 842, how does the income statement presentation of a finance lease differ from an operating lease for a lessee?

answers.text: Finance leases: single straight-line lease cost per period. Operating leases: separate interest expense and ROU amortization (front-loaded total cost)

Finance leases: separate interest expense (effective interest method on lease liability) and ROU asset amortization (generally straight-line) — total expense is front-loaded. Operating leases: single straight-line lease cost throughout the lease term
Finance and operating leases have identical income statement presentation — only the balance sheet treatment differs
Finance leases: no income statement impact until asset is sold. Operating leases: straight-line rent expense

explanations.a: This reverses the descriptions. Finance leases use separate interest and amortization (not single straight-line); operating leases use single straight-line cost.
explanations.b: Under ASC 842, finance leases produce: (1) Interest expense — computed using the effective interest method on the lease liability (higher in early periods when liability balance is largest); (2) Amortization of ROU asset — generally straight-line over the lease term or asset useful life. Total expense is front-loaded (higher in early years, declining as interest decreases). Operating leases produce: a single lease cost recognized on a straight-line basis (constant each period). This distinction affects both income statement classification and the pattern of expense recognition over the lease term.
explanations.c: The income statement presentation differs significantly between finance and operating leases — it is one of the key distinctions under ASC 842.
explanations.d: Finance lease assets are subject to ongoing amortization (not deferred until disposal). The income statement shows amortization throughout the lease term.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: Under ASC 855, the subsequent events period runs from

answers.text: The beginning of the fiscal year through the date financial statements are approved by the board of directors
The balance sheet date through the date the financial statements are available to be issued (for public entities) or are issued (for non-public entities)
The date of the auditor's report through the date the financial statements are distributed to shareholders
One year before the balance sheet date through the balance sheet date

explanations.a: The subsequent events period begins at the balance sheet date — not the beginning of the fiscal year.
explanations.b: ASC 855-10-25-1 defines the subsequent events period as the period after the balance sheet date during which management is aware of conditions or events. For SEC registrants (public companies): the period ends when financial statements are available to be issued (when all approvals are obtained). For non-public entities: the period ends when the financial statements are actually issued. Management must evaluate events occurring in this window to determine if they should be recognized or disclosed.
explanations.c: The auditor's report date is evidence of when statements were available to be issued — but the period begins at the balance sheet date, not the audit report date.
explanations.d: The subsequent events period covers the FUTURE (events after year-end), not the past. Events before the balance sheet date are reflected in the financial statements themselves.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: After the December 31 balance sheet date but before the financial statements are issued, the company's largest customer files for bankruptcy and indicates it cannot pay a $500,000 receivable balance outstanding as of December 31. This is a

answers.text: Type II (non-recognized) subsequent event — the bankruptcy occurred after year-end; disclose only

Type I (recognized) subsequent event — the customer's financial difficulties existed at December 31; the bankruptcy provides evidence of conditions existing at year-end; the receivable should be written down or fully reserved
Immaterial — customer bankruptcies are ordinary business events not requiring adjustments
A change in accounting estimate requiring prospective treatment in next year's financial statements

explanations.a: The bankruptcy provides new evidence about conditions existing at December 31 (the customer's financial difficulty). This is a recognized (Type I) event — not merely a non-recognized disclosure.
explanations.b: ASC 855-10-55-1 classifies this as a recognized subsequent event. The customer's inability to pay the $500,000 balance reflects the customer's financial condition at December 31 — the bankruptcy filing is confirmatory evidence of pre-existing conditions. Because the receivable was outstanding at year-end and the customer's difficulty existed at that date, the $500,000 receivable must be written down (or an allowance established) in the December 31 financial statements. The condition (customer's financial distress) existed at year-end; the subsequent event (bankruptcy filing) merely confirmed it.
explanations.c: $500,000 is likely material. Material receivable impairments require adjustment — not dismissal as ordinary events.
explanations.d: This is not a change in accounting estimate — it is a recognized subsequent event affecting the December 31 balance sheet.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: After the December 31 balance sheet date but before financial statement issuance, a major earthquake damages the company's primary manufacturing facility, causing $8,000,000 in losses. This is a

answers.text: Type I (recognized) subsequent event — all material post-balance-sheet losses must be accrued

Type II (non-recognized) subsequent event — the earthquake occurred after December 31; the condition (damaged facility) did not exist at year-end; disclose only without adjusting the financial statements
Ignored — natural disasters after year-end have no impact on annual financial statements
Recognized as a loss in the December 31 statements if insurance coverage is insufficient

explanations.a: The earthquake did not exist at December 31. The facility was intact at year-end — the damage arose from a new event (the earthquake) occurring after the balance sheet date. This is not a recognized event.
explanations.b: ASC 855-10-55-2 classifies the earthquake as a non-recognized subsequent event (Type II). The earthquake is a new event — not a condition that existed at December 31. The $8,000,000 loss is therefore NOT adjusted into the December 31 financial statements. However, because it is material, it must be disclosed in the notes to the December 31 financial statements: describe the nature of the event, the estimated financial effect ($8,000,000), and that the facility was damaged. Users need this information to understand the company's current financial position.
explanations.c: Material subsequent events — even non-recognized ones — require disclosure. Ignoring an $8,000,000 loss would violate ASC 855.
explanations.d: Whether insurance covers the loss affects next-year financial statements (when the loss and insurance recoveries are recognized) — not the December 31 financial statements where the event is disclosed but not recognized.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company's financial statements for the year ended December 31 were issued to the public on March 1. On March 15, the company obtains new information suggesting a previously recognized liability should be increased by $1,000,000. Under ASC 855, must the company reissue or revise its financial statements?

answers.text: Yes — all post-issuance information requires immediate restatement and reissuance
No — once financial statements are issued, events occurring after issuance are not recognized in those statements; the $1,000,000 will be recorded in the next reporting period
The $1,000,000 is reported in OCI of the subsequent period — post-issuance corrections go to OCI
The entity must file an 8-K immediately disclosing the error regardless of materiality

explanations.a: Not all post-issuance information requires restatement. Restatement is required only for errors (material misstatements from GAAP misapplication, fraud, or oversight). New information emerging after issuance that represents a new event or estimate is handled in the subsequent period.
explanations.b: The subsequent events window closes when financial statements are issued (for non-public entities) or available to be issued (for public entities). Events occurring after that date are reflected in the next reporting period's financial statements. The March 15 information arose after the March 1 issuance date — therefore, the $1,000,000 adjustment is recorded in Q1 of the following year, not in the December 31 statements. (Exception: if the March 15 information reveals an error in the December 31 statements — a misstatement from GAAP misapplication — restatement may be required under ASC 250.)
explanations.c: Post-issuance adjustments flow through net income (or retained earnings for error corrections) — not OCI.
explanations.d: SEC 8-K requirements apply to specified material events (executive departures, auditor changes, etc.) — not to all post-issuance estimate revisions. The 8-K filing is not automatically required for every liability adjustment.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A private company issues its December 31 financial statements on March 10. On February 5, a key supplier announces bankruptcy, making it unable to fulfill contracts critical to the company's operations. The company's December 31 statements show $300,000 in prepaid deposits to this supplier. How is this handled?

answers.text: No adjustment — supplier events are not subsequent events for customers

Write off the $300,000 prepaid deposit in December 31 financial statements — the supplier's bankruptcy is a recognized event providing evidence of the uncollectibility of prepaid deposits as of December 31

Disclose the bankruptcy as a Type II (non-recognized) subsequent event — the condition (supplier's financial difficulty) may not have existed at December 31; disclose the nature and potential impact without adjusting the financial statements unless evidence of pre-existing financial difficulty exists at year-end
Reduce prepaid deposits to $150,000 — a 50% reduction is the standard treatment for supplier bankruptcies

explanations.a: The supplier's bankruptcy is a material event that occurred in the subsequent events window — disclosure is required even if recognition is not.
explanations.b: Whether to recognize or disclose depends on whether the supplier's financial difficulties existed at December 31. If the bankruptcy announcement was sudden and the supplier appeared financially sound at year-end, it may be a Type II event. Additional investigation is needed.
explanations.c: This analysis is correct: The supplier's bankruptcy announced February 5 occurred in the subsequent events window (before March 10 issuance). The key question is whether the condition existed at December 31: If supplier was in financial difficulty at December 31 (Type I) → write down or reserve the $300,000 in December 31 statements. If the bankruptcy arose from new conditions after December 31 (Type II) → disclose without adjusting. The question's framing ('announces bankruptcy') suggests the condition may be new — Type II treatment with disclosure is appropriate absent evidence of pre-existing difficulty. Management must investigate and exercise judgment.
explanations.d: A fixed 50% reduction rule does not exist under GAAP. The amount recognized (if any) is based on the estimated loss — not an arbitrary percentage.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company's auditor completes the audit on February 20 (the 'dual dating' scenario). After completing the audit, but before the statements are issued on March 5, a new event occurs on February 28 that requires disclosure. The company uses dual dating. The audit report covers events through

answers.text: February 20 only — the auditor is responsible only for events through audit completion
March 5 — the auditor must review all events through the issuance date

February 20 for all events except the February 28 event, which is separately dated February 28 — dual dating limits the auditor's subsequent events responsibility for the new event to that specific date while the original audit date covers all other matters
December 31 only — subsequent events are the company's responsibility, not the auditor's

explanations.a: The auditor has responsibility through the date specified in the audit report — but dual dating extends limited responsibility for a specific new event.
explanations.b: Full extension to March 5 would require the auditor to complete additional audit procedures for all events through issuance — not just the specific new event. Dual dating avoids this broader responsibility.
explanations.c: Dual dating means the audit report is dated February 20 for all matters EXCEPT the specific new event discovered between completion and issuance — the report separately notes 'February 28 as to Note X' for the newly added disclosure. This technique: (1) preserves the February 20 audit completion date (limiting overall audit responsibility); (2) acknowledges the auditor's specific subsequent events responsibility for the February 28 event included in the financial statements; (3) is used when a subsequent event arises after audit completion but before issuance that requires disclosure or recognition.
explanations.d: Both management and the auditor have subsequent events responsibilities. Management is primarily responsible; auditors evaluate subsequent events as part of their audit procedures.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: Between December 31 and the February 15 financial statement issuance date, a company settles a lawsuit for $2,500,000. At December 31, the suit was probable and estimated at $1,800,000 (accrued as a liability). What adjustments, if any, are required in the December 31 financial statements?

answers.text: No adjustment — the $1,800,000 was properly accrued at December 31; the settlement is a next-year event
Increase the accrued liability from $1,800,000 to $2,500,000 in the December 31 statements — the settlement provides evidence of the actual loss amount as of December 31
Remove the $1,800,000 liability and recognize a gain — the lawsuit is now resolved
Increase the liability to $2,500,000 only if the $700,000 difference is material — immaterial differences are ignored

explanations.a: The settlement provides new information about a condition (the lawsuit and its likely outcome) that existed at December 31. The additional $700,000 should be recognized if material.
explanations.b: The lawsuit existed at December 31 and was being accrued. The February settlement provides better information about the December 31 liability amount — it is a recognized (Type I) subsequent event. ASC 855 requires adjusting the December 31 financial statements to reflect the $2,500,000 actual settlement amount (or disclosing if immaterial). The liability increases from $1,800,000 to $2,500,000, and additional loss of $700,000 is recognized in December 31 income. This provides users with the most accurate picture of the company's December 31 financial position.
explanations.c: The $1,800,000 liability is not reversed — it is increased to reflect the actual settlement. The lawsuit created a real obligation at December 31 that was settled for $2,500,000.
explanations.d: Materiality is a threshold for disclosure and recognition — but the principle is that the settlement provides new evidence of the actual year-end liability. If material, the full $2,500,000 must be reflected. The adjustment should be made if material; the immateriality exception applies only for truly immaterial differences.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: A company completes an initial public offering (IPO) of its common stock for $50,000,000 proceeds on January 20, after the December 31 year-end. How is this treated in the December 31 financial statements?

answers.text: Recognized in the December 31 stockholders' equity section — proceeds increase equity at year-end

Not recognized in the December 31 balance sheet (no equity entry); disclosed as a non-recognized subsequent event because the IPO occurred after December 31 and represents a new event, not evidence of a condition existing at December 31
Recognized as a liability at December 31 — proceeds received after year-end are deferred revenue
No recognition or disclosure — IPO proceeds are not material enough to warrant disclosure

explanations.a: The IPO had not occurred at December 31 — the shares had not been sold and proceeds had not been received. Recording equity from an event that had not yet happened would misstate the December 31 balance sheet.
explanations.b: The IPO on January 20 is a Type II (non-recognized) subsequent event. The IPO represents a new event arising after December 31 — not evidence of a condition existing at year-end. Therefore: (1) The December 31 balance sheet does NOT include the $50,000,000 proceeds; (2) The IPO must be disclosed in the notes to the December 31 financial statements as a significant non-recognized subsequent event — describing the nature of the offering, the proceeds, the shares issued, and any use of proceeds. This disclosure is critical given its materiality and impact on users' assessment of the company's financial position going forward.
explanations.c: IPO proceeds are equity transactions — they increase stockholders' equity when received, not a liability. But since they had not been received at December 31, no entry is appropriate.
explanations.d: A $50,000,000 IPO is unquestionably material and requires disclosure. The significance of this event to users is undeniable.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Transactions
questions.text: Which of the following subsequent events occurring between December 31 and the financial statement issuance date would be classified as a Type I (recognized) subsequent event requiring adjustment of the December 31 financial statements?

answers.text: A fire that destroys a warehouse on January 15
An acquisition of a new subsidiary completed on January 22

Resolution of a tax examination covering prior years, resulting in additional tax of $800,000 relating to December 31 and earlier periods — the IRS assessment was based on the company's tax positions as of December 31
A major decline in the company's stock price due to a broader market selloff on January 30

explanations.a: A fire on January 15 is a new event — the warehouse was intact at December 31. This is a Type II event (non-recognized): disclose, do not adjust the December 31 statements.
explanations.b: An acquisition completed January 22 is a new event — the company was not acquired at December 31. Type II: disclose without adjusting December 31 statements (unless the acquisition reveals conditions existing at year-end).
explanations.c: Resolution of a tax examination covering prior years is a classic Type I event. The IRS assessment relates to tax positions taken in periods ended on or before December 31. The tax liability existed at December 31 — the subsequent examination resolution provides new information about the amount of that liability. The $800,000 additional tax is recognized in the December 31 financial statements. This mirrors the lawsuit settlement scenario — the condition existed at year-end; the subsequent resolution provides the best estimate of the amount.
explanations.d: A post-year-end stock price decline from market conditions is a new event — market conditions at December 31 and January 30 differ. This is a Type II event requiring only disclosure if material (or no disclosure if the decline reverses or is considered normal market volatility).
